one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the Oct 2, 2015 ceremonial contract-signing and groundbreaking for the new SC complex at Fort Bonifacio, Taguig. 'Finally and at last,' the highest court of the land will own its home -- since its founding 114 years ago on June 11, 1901, the SC has been 'squatting' on UP's land and buildings on Padre Faura, Manila. Although actual construction will be undertaken and hopefully finished during the term of his successor, P-Noy -- with Senate President Drilon and Speaker Belmonte -- will be remembered in history for providing the resources. Beaming with noticeable pride, P-Noy graced the ceremony; all incumbent justices were present except Carpio (abroad on official mission) and Brion (indisposed). The three appellate courts were represented by their presiding justices -- Andres Reyes Jr. (CA), Amparo Cabotaje-Tang (SBN), Roman Del Rosario (CTA) -- and the trial courts by Court Administrator Jose Midas Marquez. But only the three lady members -- CJ Sereno, J De Castro, J Perlas-Bernabe -- delivered speeches on behalf of the Court, showing that 'though outnumbered, they are never outgunned.' Even the Court's signatory in the contract-signing was a lady -- clerk of court Felipa B. Anama. 'Women Power at work!' The male justices just sat on the stage silently witnessing the proceedings, and so did CJ. De Castro delivered the welcome remarks; Bernabe detailed the architectural plan and engineering design of the 'modern, green and disaster-resilient' complex. Taking advantage of his captive audience, P-Noy bragged that during his term the judiciary's budget more than doubled from P12.66B (2010, when he took office) to P25.89B (2016, when he will leave). Speaking in his characteristic mixture of English and Filipino, he did not mince words: 'What our bosses expect from us public servants is simple: Instead of just tiis (being patient), let's promote genuine justice. That's why I will take this opportunity to raise some issues with you.' Some serious issues he raised -- zeroing on delays and on the constitutional command that all cases or matters filed must be decided or resolved within 24 months for the SC, 12 months for all lower collegiate courts, and 3 months for all other lower courts. He was particularly distressed at the unusually long litigations involving infrastructure projects, pointing to trial courts' refusal to issue writs of possession even after the government had filed expropriation proceedings -- resulting in delays in the construction of many tollways, the NAIA expressway in particular. 'The complex that will be built will be modern and of high quality ... but for me the most important part of it is the people who will work there ... It's still up to you if you will uphold what is right and just,' he emphasized -- and attacked some decisions as 'judicial legislation.' In her speech preceding the President's, CJ Sereno highlighted five 'innovative' projects to address delays: (1) the e-Subpoena system using email to compel policemen to attend hearings, especially in drug-related cases, citing the cooperation of Secretary De Lima and former interior secretary Mar Roxas; (2) the Enterprise Information System using technology and automation to make processes faster, more efficient, transparent, and predictable; (3) the decongestion project called Hustisyeah, which reduced dockets in 119 target courts by 31.44% as of Oct 1; (4) the Assisting Court System with 47.32% docket reduction in target courts in just five months; (5) the establishment of 48 Family Courts apart from designated RTC family courts. CJ thought these five are really parts of the more extensive 'Four Pillars of Judicial Reform' the SC is undertaking -- not yet known by the public, but quickly: (1) instituting integrity, public trust, and credibility; (2) ensuring predictability, rationality, speed, and responsiveness of judicial actions; (3) improving systems infrastructure; (4) efficient and effective human resources -- promising a future column on them. Only 55, CJ Sereno has 15 more years to steer the judiciary and finish the SC complex -- she will have more time than the next two presidents to permanently reform our judicial system.
